n: T
Before giving a warning, the psalmist calls Israel to think about their God through song and dance.
T
This warning message invites Israel to worship only the Lord and to enjoy the fullness of his blessing.
T

- An Israelite tambourine was a hand drum with a round frame and skin cover. People used it as a percussion instrument during celebrations, often to accompany dancing ({{Psalm 68:25|Psalms 68:25}}; {{Psalm 149:3|149:3}}; {{Psalm 150:4|150:4}}). 

- The *sweet-sounding harp and lyre*, both stringed instruments, are the most frequently mentioned instruments in the psalms (for example, {{Psalm 33:2|Psalms 33:2}}; {{Psalm 57:8|57:8}}; {{Psalm 71:22|71:22}}; {{Psalm 150:3|150:3}}).
T

- The* ram’s horn* gathered armies and announced special holy days ({{Psalm 47:5|Psalms 47:5}}; {{Psalm 98:6|98:6}}). 

- *New Moon*: The first day of each lunar month was a festival.
T
The festival, a time to celebrate and listen to the Lord, took place at God’s appointed time.
T
*for Joseph*: The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh (the sons of Joseph) are used here to refer to the entire nation of Israel.
T
The Lord heard Israel’s cry in Egypt and rescued them from oppressive slavery.
T
God pleads with his people to remember the covenant and the Ten Commandments.
T

- God emphasizes that he and no one else rescued Israel.

- The nation should eagerly accept God's word (compare {{Deuteronomy 8:3|Deuteronomy 8:3}}; {{Ezekiel 3:1|Ezekiel 3:1}}).
T
The Lord helps Israel to understand that their failure was not because of his weakness.
T

- God wants to give his goodness to his children, but they must listen ({{Isaiah 1:18-19|Isaiah 1:18–19}}; {{Isaiah 28:12|28:12}}; {{Isaiah 48:18-19|48:18–19}}; see {{Deuteronomy 6:3|Deuteronomy 6:3}}). 

- God promises to defeat the enemies ({{Deuteronomy 9:3|Deuteronomy 9:3}}) of those who follow the paths of obedience and loyalty. He will also provide abundantly for his people ({{Isaiah 1:19|Isaiah 1:19}}).
T

- God is ready to give judgment (see {{Isaiah 3:13|Isaiah 3:13}}). 

- *divine assembly*: See {{Job 1:6|Job 1:6}}.
T
God condemns those who mistreat the helpless.
T

Because justice defines God’s rule ({{Psalm 89:4|Psalm 89:4}}), he does not support the wicked. The psalmist is confused by this situation and cries out to God to bring justice ({{Psalm 82:3-4|Psalm 82:3–4}}, {{Psalm 82:8|8}}).
T
Unjust oppressors cannot bring or restore order. They wander about in darkness, unmoved by circumstances, even when the whole world order falls apart around them (compare {{Psalm 11:3|Psalm 11:3}}).
T
The gods (see study notes on Psalm 29:1–2; 58:1), like mere humans, cannot escape the judgment common to human rulers. Jesus quoted from this passage in {{John 10:34|John 10:34}}.
T
The nations belong to God. He will take over the realms formerly ruled by local gods and give them to his people, just as he did with the promised land.
T
The enemy has successfully intimidated God’s people, so the poet prays that the Lord will hear and act.
T

This community lament asks God to rescue his people and give them victory. The short and direct poetry suggests a time of great trouble. A strong group of nations plans to destroy Israel ({{Psalm 83:1-4|Psalm 83:1–4}}) and joins together against God ({{Psalm 83:5-8|83:5–8}}). 

The psalmist remembers what happened to other enemies who attacked Israel in the past ({{Psalm 83:9-12|Psalm 83:9–12}}). He prays that the same thing will happen to these enemies ({{Psalm 83:13-16|83:13–16}}), so that they will recognize God’s power and give him honor ({{Psalm 83:17-18|83:17–18}}). 

It is not clear whether this psalm refers to one specific historical event or whether it gathers together several nations as a poetic picture of Israel’s enemies.
T
*they form an alliance*: The allies agreed to fight against God and his people. The nations named in this alliance lived around Israel and Judah.
T

- The Edomites were descendants of Esau. They lived southeast of Judah (see {{Genesis 25:30|Genesis 25:30}}; {{Genesis 32:3|32:3}}; {{Genesis 36:1-8|36:1–8}}). 

- The Ishmaelites were descendants of Hagar. They lived in the desert. 

- The Moabites and Ammonites were descendants of Lot. They lived east of Israel and Judah. 

- The Hagrites might have lived north of the Ammonites ({{1 Chronicles 5:10|1 Chronicles 5:10}}).
T

- Gebal, also known as Byblos, was on the coast of Lebanon. 

- The Amalekites lived south of Israel in the Negev desert. 

- Philistia was southwest of Judah, near the Mediterranean Sea. 

- Tyre was a port city on the Mediterranean Sea, northwest of Israel.
T

- Assyria was located northeast of Israel and north of the Persian Gulf. 

- Lot's descendants were the Moabites and the Ammonites ({{Psalm 83:6-7|Psalm 83:6–7}}).
T

The Midianites, led by Oreb and Zeeb and ruled by Zebah and Zalmunna, were Israel's enemies during Gideon's time ({{Judges 7:1-8:5|Judges 7:1–8:5}}). Barak's alliance defeated Sisera and Jabin ({{Judges 4:1-24|Judges 4}}).
T
The psalmist prays that God will miraculously destroy the new coalition as he did three other enemies; doing so would bring him glory.
T
The coalition wanted to destroy Israel to take over the land (see {{Jeremiah 3:19|Jeremiah 3:19}}).
T
*tumbleweed … chaff*: This dry plant material blows away easily (see {{Isaiah 17:13|Isaiah 17:13}}).
T
*fire … flame … tempest*: These images describe how God appears when he brings judgment (see {{Isaiah 29:6|Isaiah 29:6}}).
T
The psalmist is far from the temple. He turns toward it in hopeful reflection.
T

The psalmist deeply longs for God's presence. He feels weak with longing as he thinks about the temple and the pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem ({{Psalm 84:1-7|Psalm 84:1–7}}). He prays for himself and the community ({{Psalm 84:8-9|Psalm 84:8–9}}). 

The end of the psalm ({{Psalm 84:10-12|Psalm 84:10–12}}) shows that the temple represents God. The psalmist truly desires God's presence. He understands that God's goodness is better than life and that only God can grant his people favor and honor ({{Psalm 84:10-11|Psalm 84:10–11}}).
T
The poet envies the birds that have nesting places in and around the temple.
T
The priests and those who worked in the temple also lived there.
T
Travelers needed strength to meet the challenges of pilgrimage by foot along unpaved paths, in all kinds of weather and with the possibility of assaults.
T

The pilgrimage to Jerusalem reminded people of the exodus, when God provided for his people in a wonderful way (see {{Psalm 78:15-16|Psalm 78:15–16}}; {{Psalm 105:41|105:41}}). The psalmist describes how the hardships of the journey turn into joy when the travelers arrive.
T

- The *Valley of Baca* is also called the Valley of Weeping or the Valley of Tears. It likely symbolizes the sadness that lonely pilgrims felt (see {{Psalm 23:4|Psalm 23:4}}), rather than a real place. 

- *spring … autumn rain*: Even when pilgrims feel completely worn out, the hope of getting closer to the Lord encourages them (compare {{Isaiah 35:6-10|Isaiah 35:6–10}}; {{Isaiah 41:18-20|41:18–20}}; {{Isaiah 43:17-20|43:17–20}}; {{Isaiah 49:10|49:10}}).
T

Both kings and priests were anointed to dedicate them for service (see {{Psalm 132:17|Psalm 132:17}}; {{Exodus 28:41|Exodus 28:41}}; {{1 Samuel 9:16|1 Samuel 9:16}}; {{1 Samuel 16:1-13|16:1–13}}; compare {{Isaiah 61:1|Isaiah 61:1}}; {{Acts 10:38|Acts 10:38}}).
T
The psalmist viewed being in God’s presence as much better than being anywhere else.
T
Some people worshiped the sun as a god, but the true God provides all that anyone needs.
T
God brought Israel back from exile and restored its fortunes (see {{Psalm 14:7|Psalm 14:7}}; {{Psalm 126:1|126:1}}).
T
Though the psalmist gratefully acknowledges God’s goodness, he also asks God whether his wrath will last forever.
T

The psalmist leads the community that returned from exile in a lament and a prayer for complete restoration:

- He remembers how God rescued Israel from exile ({{Psalm 85:1-3|Psalm 85:1–3}}), 

- asks for clearer signs of God’s goodness, and

- leads the people in prayer for full renewal ({{Psalm 85:4-7|Psalm 85:4–7}}).

God answers with a message of peace ({{Psalm 85:8-9|Psalm 85:8–9}}). The psalm ends with a poetic description of the greatness of God’s salvation ({{Psalm 85:10-13|85:10–13}}).
T
When God forgave the guilt of their sins, he gave the people the possibility of fellowship with him (see {{Psalm 32:5|Psalm 32:5}}).
T
This prayer for renewal is based on God’s unfailing love for his people.
T

- When God speaks, his faithful people listen. He promises them peace, meaning wholeness and well-being (see {{Psalm 37:11|Psalm 37:11}}). They respect the Lord and know that he and his salvation are near. 

- The Lord does not tolerate foolish ways, such as those that resulted in the exile.
T

In the renewed world of salvation, all the qualities of God’s care (love, truth, righteousness, and peace) come together. They transform creation and make it new (see {{Isaiah 32:15-20|Isaiah 32:15–20}}).
T
Righteousness is like a messenger preparing the world for God’s coming in response to the prayers of his people ({{Psalm 85:4-7|Psalms 85:4–7}}; {{Psalm 89:14|89:14}}).
T
This is the only Psalm connected to David in the third book.
T
God’s devoted servant prays for mercy. The psalmist sees himself as a member of the covenant community and as a citizen of the world.
T

The psalmist cries out to God for help and praises God’s character while facing evil ({{Psalm 86:14|Psalm 86:14}}, {{Psalm 86:17|17}}). He says that all nations will one day worship the gracious and powerful God ({{Psalm 86:8-10|Psalm 86:8–10}}). Because of this hope, the psalmist commits himself to live in a right and honest way ({{Psalm 86:11|Psalm 86:11}}) and to praise the Lord ({{Psalm 86:12-13|86:12–13}}). 

The final section contrasts the behavior of evil people with the character of the Lord ({{Psalm 86:14-17|Psalm 86:14–17}}).
T

The psalmist lists God's perfect qualities ({{Exodus 34:6-7|Exodus 34:6–7}}), especially God's readiness to forgive sin (see {{Psalm 32:5|Psalms 32:5}}; {{Psalm 85:2|85:2}}; {{Psalm 145:7-10|145:7–10}}).
T
The psalmist appeals to God to remain true to his character, which is the basis for hope.
T
All the nations must submit themselves to the Lord and worship him ({{Psalm 45:17|Psalms 45:17}}; {{Psalm 117:1|117:1}}; {{Psalm 148:7-11|148:7–11}}).
T

- The poet responds to the Lord by seeking faithful instruction in the truth. 

- A person with an *undivided heart *has integrity and wholeness (see {{Psalm 73:1|Psalm 73:1}}).
T
In anticipation of God’s rescue, the psalmist praises him and trusts in his goodness.
T
Arrogant people exist both inside and outside the community. The psalmist asks God to show his character. God is so great that even a small glimpse of his goodness will silence the wicked.
T

God shows mercy to his people ({{Psalm 51:1|Psalm 51:1}}). God is compassionate ({{Psalm 25:6|Psalm 25:6}}). God is slow to become angry ({{Psalm 103:8|Psalms 103:8}}; {{Psalm 145:8|145:8}}). God is full of loving devotion and faithfulness (Hebrew *khesed* and *’emeth*; {{Psalm 143:1|Psalm 143:1}})

This verse repeats a theme first expressed in {{Exodus 34:7|Exodus 34:7}}; {{Numbers 14:18|Numbers 14:18}} (compare {{Psalm 103:8|Psalms 103:8}}; {{Psalm 145:8|145:8}}; {{Nehemiah 9:17|Nehemiah 9:17}}; {{Joel 2:13|Joel 2:13}}; {{Jonah 4:2|Jonah 4:2}}).
T
Jerusalem was Israel’s capital and the location of the temple, God’s earthly palace (see {{Psalm 84:1-12|Psalm 84}}).
T
This psalm presents Jerusalem as the city of God, where people from all nations are counted as citizens.
T

- Zion is great, but it will be even greater as an international city where believers from all nations are citizens. 

- God keeps a record of everyone who confesses him as their Lord ({{Daniel 7:10|Daniel 7:10}}; {{Revelation 13:8|Revelation 13:8}}).
T
Jerusalem becomes the international city where all God’s children are citizens.
T

- *A Maskil:* This may be a literary or musical term.

- *Heman the Ezrahite*: Heman might have been:

- a wise person from the time of King Solomon ({{1 Kings 4:31|1 Kings 4:31}}), 

- a descendant of Judah ({{1 Chronicles 2:6|1 Chronicles 2:6}}), or 

- a member of the Levite family responsible for singing at the temple ({{1 Chronicles 15:17|1 Chronicles 15:17}}; {{2 Chronicles 5:12|2 Chronicles 5:12}}).
T
The psalmist calls on the Lord for salvation.
T

In this lament, the psalmist sees himself as cast out from God’s presence. At first, he calls on the Lord. When he finds no relief from his suffering, he presents three charges against God ({{Psalm 88:6-7|Psalm 88:6–7}}, {{Psalm 88:8-12|8–12}}, {{Psalm 88:13-17|13–17}}).
T

- In his first complaint, the psalmist blames the Lord for his suffering. God’s overwhelming anger does not make sense to him.

- The phrase *the darkest of the depths* might refer to:

- the place of the dead ({{Psalm 143:3|Psalm 143:3}}; see {{Lamentations 3:6|Lamentations 3:6}}), or 

- the deep sea ({{Psalm 68:22|Psalms 68:22}}; {{Psalm 69:1-2|69:1–2}}).
T

In his second charge, the psalmist claims that God has isolated him and caused his loneliness (compare {{Psalm 31:11|Psalms 31:11}}; {{Psalm 38:11|38:11}}). In that culture, loneliness was a curse because relationships mattered more than personal success.
T
In his third charge, the psalmist accuses the Lord of rejecting him. The force and apparent cruelty of the psalmist’s suffering overwhelm him.
T
The psalmist restates his second and first charges.
T
God’s* loving devotion* gives reason to celebrate forever.
T

Book Three ({{Psalm 73:1-89:52|Psalms 73–89}}) starts and ends with serious questions. {{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}} begins with praise for how the Lord established David’s throne and kingdom ({{Psalm 89:1-37|89:1–37}}). But later the psalmist protests that the Lord seems to have rejected his covenant with David ({{Psalm 89:38-51|Psalm 89:38–51}}; see {{2 Samuel 7:8-16|2 Samuel 7:8–16}}).
T
Ethan the Ezrahite was a wise man ({{1 Kings 4:31|1 Kings 4:31}}; compare {{Psalm 88:1|Psalm 88:1}}).
T
The Lord has sworn by his own holiness ({{Psalm 89:35|Psalm 89:35}}; see {{Psalm 110:4|110:4}}).
T
The psalmist repeats God's covenant with David (see also {{Psalm 89:19-37|Psalm 89:19–37}}).
T
Those in heaven praise God's greatness (see {{Psalm 8:1|Psalm 8:1}}) because they witness his faithfulness.
T
God is the absolute standard of faithfulness, commitment, and order. The angelic beings and the heavens testify to his constancy.
T
*heavenly beings*: Literally *son of God* (see study note on Psalm 29:1–2).
T

- The Lord rules over all parts of the created order, including evil. 

- *You scattered Your enemies*: The Lord will defeat ({{Luke 1:51|Luke 1:51}}) evil forces that oppose him ({{Psalm 2:1-3|Psalm 2:1–3}}). 

- *with Your mighty arm*: This phrase represents God’s strength ({{Psalm 89:13|Psalm 89:13}}).
T
In this hymn, the psalmist celebrates God’s complete and powerful rule over nature.
T
Mount Tabor was in northern Israel. Mount Hermon formed the extreme northern border of the nation.
T
God rules wisely over creation. The qualities of righteousness, justice, and faithfulness fit the description of a wise ruler. The happy people who live under his rule enjoy his protection.
T
Those who are wise worship God, walk in his light, rejoice in their relationship with him, and delight in his character.
T
The Lord protects his people with the same power by which he established the created order.
T
The Lord chose David as his son and king of Israel (see {{Psalm 2:4-6|Psalm 2:4–6}}; {{2 Samuel 7:8-16|2 Samuel 7:8–16}}) to protect his people.
T
*I have anointed him*: This is the verb from which comes *anointed one* (Hebrew *mashiakh*, which means “messiah”).
T

The Lord adopted David as his son, appointed him as his commander over the nations, and promised to support him forever. Verse 26 recalls a verse from David’s song of praise ({{2 Samuel 22:47|2 Samuel 22:47}}).
T
David would become the greatest of earthly kings. The Hebrew word translated *highest* is the same word used for God as “Most High” (*‘elyon*).
T

The Lord displays his faithfulness in the heavens, across his whole creation (see {{Psalm 89:2|Psalm 89:2}}). In the same way, he confirms his commitment to the kings that would come from David's family.
T

The Lord disciplines his children when they go astray, but he does not reject them. He knows they will break their trust and will need correction, yet he remains committed to keep his covenant. His faithfulness to David is like his faithfulness to the created world.
T

*holiness*: The Lord is completely different from the created world ({{Psalm 22:3|Psalm 22:3}}). His character is entirely pure. He acts according to his will ({{Psalm 115:3|Psalm 115:3}}) and chooses to be faithful ({{Psalm 89:1|89:1}}; {{Psalm 115:1|115:1}}). Therefore, he cannot lie.
T
*You are enraged*: The psalmist is confused by the severity of God's anger.
T
*broken down all his walls*: The Lord’s people are completely vulnerable.
T
Although the Lord promised to strengthen David, he has made David’s enemies strong
T
The psalmist wonders whether he will live long enough to see the Lord’s anger end. Human life is short and passes quickly before the Lord ({{Psalm 90:4|Psalm 90:4}}, {{Psalm 90:10|10}}).
T
The phrase *Your servants *refers to the community loyal to the Lord.
T

This doxology (a short praise to God) ends Book Three of the Psalms ({{Psalm 73:1-89:52|Psalms 73–89}}). It was not meant to be read as part of {{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}}. Its words of praise stand in strong contrast to the pain and questions expressed in {{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}}. Compare {{Psalm 41:13|Psalm 41:13}}; {{Psalm 106:48|106:48}}.
T

- Moses led God's people from slavery in Egypt to Mount Sinai. There, he received the law and established God's covenant with Israel. 

- *the man of God*: Moses had a special relationship with God ({{Deuteronomy 33:1|Deuteronomy 33:1}}).
T

The Lord is the* dwelling place* for the godly. He has provided shelter for many generations. The word translated as *dwelling place* is rare in the Psalms. It describes a safe place where the Lord meets and cares for those in need ({{Psalm 68:5|Psalms 68:5}}; {{Psalm 71:3|71:3}}).
T

Although the Lord’s people have lived in him for many generations, their sin creates distance between them and their eternal Lord. The Lord’s anger against human sin can seem to last a lifetime. Even then, it is only a small sign of his full displeasure with sin. This sad situation leads the community to seek the Lord’s light.

The first step is to ask the Lord to restore them because of his compassion and faithful love ({{Psalm 90:13-14|Psalm 90:13–14}}). He alone can make his servants glad. He alone can bless the generations that come after them ({{Psalm 90:16-17|Psalm 90:16–17}}).
T

- The Lord is the eternal God. 

- The Lord created the earth.
T
Unlike God, humans are mortal and temporary.
T
Sinners cannot escape God’s anger against sin because the Lord sees their sins. Their lives pass quickly and are full of suffering.
T

- A groan of sorrow ({{Ezekiel 2:10|Ezekiel 2:10}}) represents a life facing the consequences of sin. 

- Humans create trouble (see {{Psalm 10:6|Psalm 10:6}}) and receive pain as a result.
T

In the search for wisdom, no one can fully understand the Lord (see {{Isaiah 40:13|Isaiah 40:13}}). The right human response to the Lord is godly fear (see {{Psalm 60:4|Psalm 60:4}}). The Lord alone can teach humans to follow the path of wisdom ({{Psalm 25:4-6|Psalm 25:4–6}}).
T
The phrase *Your servants* refers to the community of those loyal to the Lord.
T
The psalmist prays for the Lord’s favor and restoration.
T
The psalmist calls upon the Lord to give the people gladness to replace their mourning (see {{Psalm 92:4-5|Psalm 92:4–5}}).
T
The *children* represent future generations in contrast to the generations past ({{Psalm 90:1|Psalm 90:1}}).
T
Humans waste their efforts unless the Lord makes them successful ({{Psalm 44:3|Psalm 44:3}}).
